To rejuvenate something or someone means to bring back a sense of youth, energy, freshness, or strength — especially after a period of tiredness, aging, or decline.

The heart of this word is the idea of going back to a better, more vibrant state. Something was once full of life or energy. It lost that quality. Then, something happens to bring that quality back. That process — that restoration of liveliness — is what rejuvenate describes.

Think of it as: "You had it. You lost it. Now it's back."
Breaking It Down with a Simple Image

Imagine a wilting plant. Its leaves are drooping, its color has faded, it looks tired and lifeless. Then you water it, give it sunlight, and move it to a better spot. Over a few days, it perks up, turns bright green, and looks alive and healthy again.

That process of coming back to life — that is rejuvenation. If you caused that transformation, you rejuvenated the plant.

Now scale that image up. It could be a person, a city, a company, a relationship, a piece of music — anything at all. The word works the same way.
Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. Rejuvenating a Person

When used for people, it means making someone feel younger, more energetic, more alive — physically, mentally, or emotionally.

  • "A week of sleep and rest completely rejuvenated him."
  • "The vacation rejuvenated her spirit."
  • "A cold shower in the morning rejuvenates me."

Notice that it doesn't have to mean the person literally becomes younger. It means they feel as if they have — they feel lighter, sharper, more energetic, more alive.

2. Rejuvenating a Place, Organization, or Thing

When used for something non-human, it means bringing new life, energy, or improvement to something that had become old, dull, stagnant, or run-down.

  • "The government spent millions to rejuvenate the old city center." (buildings repaired, parks created, new businesses opened)
  • "The new manager rejuvenated the struggling company." (fresh ideas, renewed motivation, better performance)
  • "New players rejuvenated the aging football team."
A Crucial Nuance: It Implies a Real, Significant Transformation

Rejuvenate is not a light word. You wouldn't say a single cup of tea "rejuvenated" you — that would be an exaggeration. The word carries weight. It suggests a meaningful, noticeable change, not a small, temporary lift. It implies that something was noticeably tired, worn, or declining — and now it has been meaningfully revived.

Compare:

  • "A quick nap refreshed me." → small, short boost ✔
  • "A month-long holiday in the mountains rejuvenated me completely." → deep, significant restoration ✔
Common Forms You'll See in Sentences

• "She rejuvenated the neighborhood." (active — she caused the change)
  • "The neighborhood was rejuvenated." (passive — the change happened to it)
  • "She felt rejuvenated after the retreat." (very common — describing how someone feels after being restored)
  • "It was a rejuvenating experience." (used as an adjective — describing what caused the feeling)

The passive form — "felt rejuvenated" — is extremely common in everyday speech, so pay attention to it.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are related, but not identical:

  • Refresh — a lighter, smaller boost. A glass of water refreshes you. A full month of rest rejuvenates you. Refresh is everyday; rejuvenate is bigger and deeper.
  • Revive — to bring something back from near death or collapse. It has a more urgent, rescue-like feeling. You revive someone who fainted. You rejuvenate someone who has been worn down over time.
  • Restore — to return something to its original condition. Restore is more neutral and technical (you restore a painting, restore a file). Rejuvenate is warmer and specifically implies energy and youthfulness coming back.
  • Revitalize — the closest synonym to rejuvenate. They are nearly interchangeable, but rejuvenate has a slightly stronger suggestion of youth specifically, while revitalize focuses more on vitality and energy in general.

Almost anything that can lose energy, freshness, or vitality can be rejuvenated:

  • Body — "Exercise and good sleep rejuvenated his body."
  • Mind — "Reading rejuvenates my mind."
  • Skin — "This cream claims to rejuvenate aging skin." (very common in beauty products)
  • Cities and neighborhoods — "The council plans to rejuvenate the old docks."
  • Companies and brands — "They hired a new designer to rejuvenate the brand."
  • Teams and groups — "Young talent rejuvenated the squad."
  • Economies — "Investment in infrastructure rejuvenated the local economy."
  • Relationships — "The trip together rejuvenated their marriage."
  • Culture and art — "The new movement rejuvenated classical music."

Rejuvenate is a positive, hopeful word. It is never used negatively. Wherever you see it, it signals that something good has happened — that energy, life, and freshness have been won back. It carries a sense of renewal and optimism.

It is used in both formal and informal settings — in newspapers, in medical and wellness contexts, in business writing, and in everyday conversation.
One Final Sentence to Lock It In

"After years of feeling exhausted and burned out, the long rest in the mountains completely rejuvenated her — she returned home feeling young, energetic, and ready to take on the world again."

That single sentence captures everything: the prior state of decline, the process of restoration, and the outcome — a return to youthful energy and vitality. That is rejuvenate in its fullest sense.
